title: Cross runtime Solution to Enable C# Web Exports
body:
## Cross‑runtime C# web exports via direct WASM interop

### Summary

This PR adds an optional module that lets C# game scripts run in the browser together with Godot. The two runtimes share the same thread and call each other's WASM exports synchronously. The C# usage is similar to GodotSharp but not yet same as it. I also tried as much as possible in C# to mirror Godot Types as implemented in GodotSharp.

### How it works

- Godot boots on the main thread, then .NET 10 boots after it.
- A JavaScript bridge (`__callGodot`) is installed. Every C# method call goes through `[JSImport]` to the bridge, which marshals the arguments and calls the right EMSCRIPTEN_KEEPALIVE C++ function.
- The C++ side recovers the live object from the raw pointer, looks up the method bind, and runs it. The result is decoded and handed back to C#.

### Boot sequence

1. User clicks → Godot starts.
2. JS bridge modules are loaded.
3. `__callGodot` is defined on the main thread.
4. .NET runtime boots via `dotnet.js`.
5. `InitInterop()` walks the scene tree and caches node references.
6. Signal forwarding (`_crossRuntimeNotifyCSharp`) and the frame step (`__stepFrame`) are wired up.
7. The game loop runs: each frame Godot calls `__stepFrame(delta)`, C# logic runs synchronously and control returns to Godot.

### Call path

```
C# method call  
- [JSImport] GodotBridge.CallGodot(fn, object[] args)  
- __callGodot looks up the signature in GODOT_EXPORT_SIGNATURES  
- marshals arguments into Godot's heap  
- calls the Godot WASM export  
- C++ reconstructs arguments, executes the method bind  
- return value is decoded by JS and sent back to C#
```

### Why the earlier worker approach was dropped

The first version of this module ran .NET in a Web Worker, communicating with Godot over a SharedArrayBuffer. It used fixed memory offsets for commands and data, plus atomics for status polling.

That approach worked but had two big problems which i observed in godot mono pong version:
1. The constant crossing between threads added latency on every call. 
2. The status‑polling design meant C# had to spin‑wait for Godot to finish before it could continue, which blocked the worker and limited throughput. The whole thing felt sluggish.

I eliminated the worker thread approach as Emscripten also does not allow calling into the Godot module from a worker – the module's exports are only reachable on the main thread. So the worker had no direct access to Godot functions. It had to write commands into the shared buffer and then signal the main thread to process them. That extra hop added both complexity and delay.

I also had to add `-sEXPORT_ALL=1` in the link flags in platform/web/detect.py in order to eliminate lazy wrapper wasm exports which occassionaly resulted in function mismatches and to also expose some functions I needed to make it work.

The performance improvement is significant (I visually compared the frame smoothness and input latency against the Godot Mono editor running the same Pong demo. The direct‑call version felt much more similar to the native editor but not quite there yet. Its still noticeably slower.). Profiling will be done in the follow up.

### Argument marshalling

- Primitives (`bool`, `int`, `float`, `string`) pass as-is.
- Structs (`Vector2`, `Color`, `Transform3D`, etc.) are flattened into primitives.
- Packed arrays use bulk memory copies via `Span<byte>`.
- Callables are flattened into `(targetId, method)`.
- Arrays and Dictionaries pass a pointer table of Variants and an element count.
- Varargs are passed as a pointer table of Variants, with a heuristic that resolves integer values in the WASM address range to Object pointers.

### Return values

- Primitives are decoded directly from the Variant result.
- Structs come back as JS objects with named fields; C# reassembles them.
- Packed arrays are returned as `object[]` and converted element‑wise.
- Objects are returned as raw pointers; C# constructs the wrapper object with that pointer.
- Object instance IDs cross the boundaries as pointer values to avoid precision problems in JavaScript and .NET. It also avoids specialized serialization on the two sides.

### API generation

The whole class API is generated from `extension_api.json` by three Python scripts:

- `cpp_generators.py` – one C++ file per class, every method as a flat EMSCRIPTEN_KEEPALIVE export.
- `gen_cs.py` – one C# wrapper class per Godot class, with methods, properties, signals, and singleton access.
- `js_generator.py` – emits `export_signatures.js`, a static map of every function's parameter and return kinds, used by the marshaler at runtime.


### Signals

A C++ singleton (`CrossRuntimeEventSignal`) intercepts connected signals and forwards them to C# via `_crossRuntimeNotifyCSharp`. The C# side subscribes with normal event syntax:

```csharp
ball.BodyEntered += OnBodyEntered;
```

### Testing

- Most of the testing was based on simple game scripts.
- There is not yet any automated testing.

### AI usage disclosure
I utilized AI in the writing of the C# and C++ generators, the SignalManager and the repetitive sections of the JavaScript Marshal. The architectural decisions, the interop design, the memory debugging, the type codec were done manually. I understand every line of code in this submission.

### Known limitations

- GD class is not yet fully completed.
- In Godot types, some methods have not been implemented.
- Enum names are uppercased to avoid C# collisions (`KeyModifierMask` becomes `KEYMODIFIERMASK`). This differs from GodotSharp but eliminates the need for an "Enum" suffix.
- The ergonomics are not yet the same as a godotsharp experience.
- Methods that collide with signal names are dropped.
- The vararg heuristic could misidentify large integer literals as pointers, though valid WASM addresses make this extremely unlikely. In the event it does, the get instance id check will fail to get the instance id which means it will end up being treated as an integer.
- No CI tests yet; all testing is manual.
- Performance has not yet been profiled for a reliable comparison. 
- For resource referencing, I added a hashtable which references created resources. I haven't created the release mechanism for it yet. 
- There are a significant number of warnings in C# which will be sorted out in the next iteration.

> Please note that this is still a work in progress.

I would appreciate feedback on:
1. Review of the overall architecture – especially the direct‑call approach vs. the earlier shared‑memory prototype.
2. The cleanest way to integrate the code‑generation step into the build step. I included extensions_api.json in the commit.
3. Any other changes or improvements you'd like to see.
4. Where I am going wrong and whether this is an approach that makes sense.


Happy to discuss and adjust anything.
